utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and, together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Oric. We have with us here our legal assistants, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, mad ham and good morning to you and your team. So before we start with the evidence of today's witness let me just make a statement relating to developments during the recess. And in particular, I wish to state that upon our or as per our instructions, last week, our Senior Legal Officer presided over a 65 ter meeting to gather information from the parties and also discuss with the parties on our behalf the proposed continuation and finalisation of these proceedings. This 65 ter Conference was held last Friday, the 13th, and I'm informed by Mr. Von Hebel not only of the various points discussed but also that the 65 ter Conference itself went very well. I will try to touch upon some of the issues raised and some of the developments that have been registered today, and leave some others for later. The idea is that we try and start with the testimony of today's witness as early as we can. Now, the first matter that emerged from the 65 ter meeting to which I expect to be a follow-up -- there to be follow-up today is that after due consideration, the Defence have decided to call only four of the remaining witnesses to testify viva voce here and that is Suhra -- she does not have any protective measures, does she? Yeah, okay. Suhra Djilovic, who will testify today, Ejub Guster, your expert Professor Bilic, and Lieutenant Colonel Fenzel. In all, the testimony of these individuals, these four individuals, is expected to take the remainder of this week and the next. We anticipate to finish on the 26th or the 27th. We will try to do our utmost to finish on the 26th because on the 27th there is a problem. Then there are two other individuals to which, or about which the Defence have got submissions. One is a certain Philip Von Rechlinghousen. He is the subject of a Rule 92 bis motion. We will be handing down the decision -- deciding this morning. Our decision would roughly require you to have his statement sworn according to procedure and then, of course, it will be admitted also because there is no other kind of objection on the part of the Prosecution. There is, it seems, a problem with the other person, Dr. Paul Cornish, the military analyst, and your proposal was to put him as subject of a motion under Rule 94 bis. I know that this issue was raised during the 65 ter meeting. The indication that I have from our Senior Legal Officer is that the Prosecution intimated that they would be asking for the production of this gentleman to come forward for cross-examination. In other words, that it would not be plain sailing procedure under Rule 94 bis by simply filing the expert report of this gentleman. So what I would like from you now is to confirm to me what the situation is as regards the following two points. On the part of the Defence, whether the position remains as you put it to the Senior Legal Officer last Friday, in other words, that there are four remaining witnesses to come forward and testify viva voce and as regards the Prosecution, what's your position formally in relation to Dr. Paul Cornish and, since I was given to understand by the Senior Legal Officer that if the Prosecution maintains their position with regard to this person, you will -- you might consider withdrawing him from being one of your expert witnesses. I would then please ask you to confirm or reconsider your position. So Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones, are you confirming to the Trial Chamber that you have got basically four remaining viva voce witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And as far as Dr. Cornish is concerned, it's not really that there was a problem with his -- him testifying, it's simply that we decided that if there were no opposition to his report from the Prosecution, then we would submit his report in which case he would need to remain on the list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If they opposed them, then of course we do drop him and essentially we are waiting for the Prosecution to -- formally to reply or to respond to our motion and then we would act accordingly but Your Honour understands the position exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that. Yes, Mr. Wubben, thank you. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I confirm that our position remained that we want to cross-examine the expert by the Defence, Dr. Cornish, and we will formalise our opinion, of course, by motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Mr. Jones, that's the position confirmed by the Prosecution. Basically what -- I'm just repeating it, for no other reason except that if that is the case, you might consider dropping this witness now so that he won't have to file a motion in any case and we won't have to decide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it will remain on record that they insisted and that is the reason for the dropping of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we can certainly do that, indicate now that we would drop him. I just mention one thing which is one of the reasons why we filed the report even though we were considering not calling Dr. Cornish during the Defence case is that if the Prosecution were to call a military expert in rebuttal, we might want to call him in rejoinder, and given the time periods under 94 bis we thought it best to file it as early as possible. So it was the right to apply to bring him in rejoinder that we drop him for our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So basically, that means that you only need to attend to the -- to formalising the von Rechlinghousen statement according to our procedure. That would be admitted as evidence under Rule 92 bis. And we will, of course, proceed with the testimony of the four remaining witnesses. I know because I had asked Mr. Von Hebel to deal with this matter with you during the 65 ter meeting, the question of rebuttal. He reported to me that somehow you were taken by surprise, Mr. Wubben, by the fact that the number of Defence witnesses was being reduced to four viva voce and one, maximum two, under Rule 92 bis, and that you stated to Mr. Von Hebel that, although you had, of course, been giving a question of rebuttal, something you were not in a position there, and then to come forward with the necessary information. Mr. Von Hebel informs me that you indicated that you would be in a position to come back to the Tribunal on this matter either today or tomorrow. Are you in a position to enlighten us on whether there will be -- whether to expect a rebuttal, what kind of rebuttal -- in other words, who will be coming over and, of course, I do concede that the need might arise for adding or even subtracting from your rebuttal following the testimony of the remaining viva voce witnesses, so -- of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, over the weekend we were not able to contact the potential witnesses for rebuttal but we have at least isolated five issues, including the possibility of an expert on handwriting for a rebuttal on those parts of the expert report by Mr. Bilic that are not -- that are new as a kind of expertise. So meaning that are not a -- in a stage or a label of a contra expertise but a new expertise by expert Bilic regarding certain documents. The other issues involved are local commandership, the role of the military police, and the credibility of a witness. We tried to at least to get one witness via a 92 bis or 89(F), and we tried to minimise it to that extent and I forgot that we also would like to call a witness in rebuttal for identifying an image. Now, I know I'm aware of the fact that I am now limited at this very moment but we are still in the phase of contacting these witnesses for their availability to testify in court at this stage. So far we were not successful but we will continue today and I might update you further tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. May I just make things clear, because I don't want to fall on you with surprises in due course. Our plan is to start with the rebuttal, if there will be one, on the 30th of this month. In other words -- Monday. A Tuesday? The 31st, yeah, to start on Tuesday, the 31st. So you don't have much time. I mean, I think the identification of the remaining witnesses in rebuttal that you may have, do not need to wait until now to start with. And secondly, I mean, you need to move because come what may, on the 31st, if you have them available, we'll start. If you don't have them available, we'll move on, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is in relation to this handwriting expert that additional handwriting expert that we reserve our position on that and the main reason is the following: That I was going to announce later on today, but I'll make the announcement now, that things being what they are, in other words since we have two reports by expert hand writer -- handwriting experts, one from your part and one from the Defence part, which are almost 100 per cent diametrically opposed and since the last thing on earth that we would pretend is to know anything about the subject ourselves, we have met over the holidays, and discussed and confirmed amongst ourselves yesterday, that we will be appointing an expert in handwriting ourselves. That is the position. It's being worked upon by the Registrar. We handed down lists of possible experts yesterday but, of course, these are all busy people and they are being -- the list is being examined by the Registrar. I expect some kind of feedback later on this morning, after which I will come back to you after having discussed further with my two colleagues. If there are further documents that you need to be examined, I think you need to sit down and realise that it makes much more sense that you tell us which documents you're interested in at this stage so that we ourselves refer them to this independent expert rather than ask that you bring forward once more an ex parte expert which would only serve as an invitation for the other party to bring over another expert -- ex parte expert on their part and then ultimately probably a further decision on our part to appoint again independent experts from our part. So, please, be sensible about it. Of course, I am reserving your position and ours when it comes to -- when it comes to your requests for rebuttal and for the Defence's request for rejoinder. Do please keep in mind what I have just told you. Later on, I will, after consultation with my two colleagues, inform you more in detail about the terms of reference of the expert but our idea is that the expert will start working on the assignment that we will give him or her or them because ideally if we could have more than one expert it will be even better, more than one expert that would work independently of each other and then present a joint report, if necessary. There is, however, a problem that has arisen this morning in this context, which I think I better mention now, and that is the following, that I have been informed by a member of my staff that the Defence has asked the Prosecution to make available for the duration of the testimony of Professor Bilic the originals of the nine documents, P74, 73, 75, P4, P37, P158, P14, P10, and P3. Now, you will understand that if these are needed for the purpose of Mr. Bilic's testimony, we cannot refuse this; we would rather ask them to make them available. But if they are here for the duration of the testimony of Professor Bilic, then obviously they cannot be available at the same time to the expert that we are going to appoint. So I'm saying this without in any way interfering with what might be going on between you. If they need to be here, of course, they will be here and they will be made available to our expert later. That would only delay things but in the meantime, it could also help matters in the sense that you'll be able to identify in the meantime any further documents or exhibits that you might wish to be examined by our expert/experts that we will be appointing. All right? Any comments on your parts, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, just in terms of the originals being available I'm afraid we do need those. In proofing the witness it's clear that he -- in fact, he insists on having them and will show watermarks and things which can only be shown with the originals. So that is the position as far as that's concerned. I did wonder whether we would be given the opportunity to address Your Honour on the terms of reference and the nationality of the expert, the procedure and protocol, whether we would have time, well, certainly to, of course, first of all cross-examine the witness and therefore also to submit the court's expert report to our expert so that we can take instructions as to how to cross-examine him there are lots of matters of procedure and protocol that you need to hear from us on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think the terms of reference are our business and not the parties', obviously, but since you feel that there is a need for you to make submissions - and I don't know what's the position of the Prosecution - of course, we will be very glad to hear your submissions. Ultimately, we were thinking in our discussions on this matter, trying to save on time as much as we can, we were thinking about the possibility of ultimately having the expert or experts that we will appoint to come here and present his, her, or their report orally rather than necessarily in writing. The reason is we'll save time. You will, of course, have every opportunity to examine or cross-examine, call it whatever you like, to put questions to our expert or experts, and we also discussed amongst ourselves yesterday that since you are more or less in our same position, in other words I would take it that you know about the subject as much as we do, that you would require some kind of assistance to enable you to put questions to our expert or experts, in which case we would be very glad to hear submissions on your part on what your requirements would be and, of course, we will come forward with our response in due course but we do acknowledge that -- I mean, I was Defence counsel myself in years gone, and, of course, I needed expert advice and assistance to be able to put questions to court-appointed experts on various matters, not just on handwriting. So we would be very pleased to hear your submissions on the matter and we will give our reactions after due consultation and discussion. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So I take it firstly I won't make the submissions now. Obviously that will be in due course and in fact it might even be better after our expert has testified depending on your schedule because there are points I would make in light of his evidence about the nature of any further examination. I think we would need at that time a minimum him our expert present at the Bench with us when it comes to examining the Court's expert but that's a matter which we can address subsequently. One other matter I just wanted to mention, Your Honour, is that we share absolutely the concern to move on to the subsequent stages of this trial, rebut and rejoinder, as soon as possible but without that in any way that -- the routine-ness of that impinging on our right obviously to object that witnesses proposed by the Prosecution in rebuttal should have been called earlier. For example, we may wish to argue that, I don't know, for the role of the military police that that's not an appropriate matter for rebuttal, that it should have been dealt with earlier. I'm not making that submission now but we certainly want to have the time to make those submissions and also we, of course, need to prepare and investigate any proposed witnesses by the Prosecution. Just as in during the Prosecution case, that involves investigations in the field, involves us making our own inquiries so naturally this does take time and, if witnesses from the Prosecution start immediately after the Defence case, I fear we may not have time to prepare for that. I make that point now and we will wait for the motion from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what the Prosecution is coming up with in any case, Mr. Jones, so obviously I will put no questions to you with regard to rejoinder now because that very much depends on the position which will be taken by the Prosecution. Then there are issues as relate -- that relate to disputed exhibits. I am informed and I wish to have a confirmation of it now, that towards the -- after that you finished with your four remaining witnesses, you intend to -- still intend to file the documents indicating the nature of your objection to the disputed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, that's not exactly the position. It's that at the end of the evidence we can submit and not a motion - I'm not sure if it should be described as a motion - a statement but as long as there is still evidence including from the Court-appointed expert that would be something that would be incorporated in this document obviously. So for example if the Court appointed expert finds that one of those documents is suspicious that's obviously something we would add to our filing so only at the very end I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That will be extremely important to us. The other thing is that we were discussing this yesterday, amongst ourselves, the question of the translation of some exhibits, particularly the war diary, P84, if I remember well, and also of what is purported to be the Accused's interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, where there have been several allegations that the translation as it appears in the transcript is not correct. I'm not going to say more than that. I hope that together with several other issues that you are paying this all due attention. The other thing, Mr. Wubben, I want to conclude on this matter, if possible today. The last day we sat before the Christmas recess, you asked for leave to remove Exhibit 561 for the purpose of forensic examination. We decided it orally, gave you permission to do so. It's a month now. Basically the 19th of December is when this happened. What is the position? Has the -- are you still in possession of Exhibit 561? Has it been returned? Have there been any forensic examination? If there have been, is this going to be the subject of further evidence? What's the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I please confirm? Will you please bear me a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Patricia Sellers will make a submission in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, sorry, Ms. Sellers, sorry, Mr. Wubben, yes, I was helping Judge Eser. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. In relationship to document Prosecution Exhibit 561 we will be returning it today. It is in our possession and we would like to announce to the Trial Chamber, also to the Defence, that it was not the subject of forensic analysis and so that will not be any additional evidence that we will be putting before the Trial Chamber, and there were technical reasons why we could not proceed on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So in other words, there will not be any evidence coming forward on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, only in relationship to the forensic analysis of the document. The document we still believe is a relevant piece of evidence from the Prosecution and that we will -- potential that we will be using that evidence in the further cross-examination of Defence witnesses but only in terms of a forensic report related to the document. It is in that manner that we will not be going for -- with additional forensic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But that's what I meant, yeah. All right. So that matter is closed. May I also inform you that later on this morning, during the break, because there were some technical hitches that made it impossible for me this morning to sign these motions, we will be signing the -- I'll be signing the Rechlinghousen, as I said, decision, and also two other decisions that we discussed and decided upon in the course of the recess. One is on the Defence motion regarding the consequences of failing to put its case to witnesses pursuant to Rule 90(H)(ii), and the other one in relation to the Defence motion regarding documents from Republika Srpska OBS [phoen] source, and those will be decided later on. I think I have covered -- yes. The other thing that I want to know is, the end of -- let's start -- the end of Defence case, rebuttal, rejoinder, any time that may be needed to conclude the question of the report of the expert that we may not -- not that we will be appointing, the handwriting expert. And reserving, of course, your rights if there will be any left on evidentiary -- at the evidentiary level after that. And we will obviously come to a stage when we will start with the proceedings that usually follow that stage. In other words, for the preparation of the final briefs until closing arguments, et cetera. I know that Mr. Von Hebel discussed this with you, and the -- I just want a confirmation from you that past the stage that I mentioned earlier, in other words when everything has been cooked, ready for eating, in other words that you will -- that you are happy with the time frame that was put to you by Mr. Von Hebel on our behalf. Mr. Jones and Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we are happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Good. So there are other issues that came up during the 65 ter meeting and that I could mention now but I think we better start with the witness, and later on, between now and the end of next week, I will raise these issues with you as we go along and try to save time today on -- in that way. All right? Yes. Any further issues that you would like to raise before I call in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Only to update you that today we will file our 94 bis(B) motion regarding the expert Bilic. Still has to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. Okay. Thank you. Usher, please. Now, are arrangements already in place to have her facial -- face distorted, facial appearance distorted? We don't have to go into closed session or open session as she walks in? No? That's what I want to make sure in other words because she will be walking in I suppose from here to her place over there and I want to make sure that if there are cameras operating at the time she will not be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. For your information, also, on January the 24th, that's Tuesday today week, because of the limited space that we have available and which has to be shared between the various Trial Chambers -- yes, bring her in, please. Oric will stop at roughly 11, 11.30, and then I need to preside over another case. So that's for your information. If on the 23rd, that's the day before, we realise that we still need that hour or so that we will be otherwise losing, then I would suggest to you that instead of starting at nine we start at eight in the morning on that Tuesday, all right? So I'm just alerting you to this and keep your eyes open as we go along. Yes, Madam, good morning to you. And on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and myself I'd like to welcome you to this Tribunal. You are going to start giving evidence in this case, which has been instituted against Naser Oric. Our Rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in the piece of paper that Madam Usher is handing to you now. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth and nothing but the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like the cameraman to focus on the witness for a brief moment so that I explain something to her. Yes, Madam, if you look at the monitor in front of you, that is how you are seen outside these four walls. In other words, as per your request as communicated to us by the Defence, the Defence team for Mr. Oric, we have agreed to hide your face from public -- from the public, and therefore the public, who may be following these proceedings outside these four walls, will only be able to see what you are seeing now on the monitor. In other words, no one will be able to recognise your face. That should make it easier for you and more comfortable to start and proceed with your testimony. The procedure here is a very simple one. You will be first asked questions by Madam Vidovic, who is lead counsel for Mr. Oric, since you are a Defence witness, and when she is finished you will then be asked questions by Ms. Sellers from the Prosecution team. Your responsibility under the solemn undertaking that you have made with us is that you answer all questions put to you, independently and irrespective of who is putting the question to you, in a truthful manner, and as fully as possible. When I say as fully as possible, I would like you to avoid beating around the bush and giving us information that has not been asked from you. Please restrict your answers to what is being asked. In other words, my advice to you is to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. That way you will be able to walk out of this courtroom and go back home as early as possible. Throughout the proceedings, you will be receiving interpretation in your language. For example, I'm speaking in English now, but -- I'm talking in English but as I go along, everything that I say will be translated to you in Serbo-Croat. If you have at any time problems with interpretation, please draw our attention straight away and we will rectify it, all right? Okay. Thank you. Madam Vidovic will be asking you questions and both of you will be using the same language, so Madam Vidovic will now give you a piece of very important advice, which I invite you to follow. Otherwise I will see very many unhappy faces behind the glass panes that there are behind you. Those are the interpreters, and everything that is being said by you and by Madam Vidovic in your own language needs to be translated to us in English. So if you don't allow -- and in French. If you don't allow a short interval of time between question and answer, they will have problems and we will not be exactly very happy. So Madam Vidovic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As His Honour said we speak the same language, so I wish to ask you to pause after each one of my questions to make it possible for the interpreters to interpret correctly my question and your answer. I will do my best to make a pause, too. First I will ask you to tell Their Honours your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Suhra Djilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your maiden last name is Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 18th of October 1956 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your father's name was Ramo and your mother's Habiba, nee Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You completed primary school in 1970 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you went to secondary school for economics which you completed in 1975 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From 1982, you worked at various administrative jobs in the municipal administrative organs in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The war found you in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You spent the entire war in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You left Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm having a lot of problems in hearing through the head set.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the same problems, Witness?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hear some sounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let -- let's do it. Let me get an idea of what kind of sounds you're talking about. The B/C/S is number 6. Could I ask you, Madam Vidovic, to proceed onward with another question. We'll repeat it later but I want to possibly understand what this sound is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You left Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the tragedy that occurred in July 1995 in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that tragedy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The idea was to try and understand so I actually switched on to channel 6, which is the channel you are following, and I have an indication there is a kind of an echo, a background echo. It's as if one could hear other people talking. I don't know exactly what it is, so perhaps we could have some assistance. It has happened in the past and the way we solved it was to put down the volume. Are you still encountering the same problem now, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try, Your Honour. No. It's better now. I think it's better now. We shall see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You, Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Da what? Are you still --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better now. I can understand better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's better, okay. All right. So I think we have more or less solved it. Since I was not following completely what you were asking of the witness because I was interested in trying to find a solution to the problem, could I now invite you, Madam Vidovic, to repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the tragedy that occurred when Srebrenica fell, you lost your husband, brother, your sister lost her family, and you lost many family members, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just before the war broke out, you were working at administrative jobs in the municipal Secretariat for All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness Defence Exhibit? It's a document issued by the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica, and the ERN is 01830891. The date on the document is the 15th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at the document when you receive it. The document at the end has the name of the Staff Commander, Suljo Hasanovic, and the secretary, Nurija Porobic. I will quote part of the document to you. Please look at paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 4, 5 and 6. It says, in the document, in the area of Srebrenica municipality, the municipal staff of the TO Srebrenica was established with 22 conscripts as well as the staff protection company with 55 conscripts. Also, the detachment in the following composition was formed and it goes on with a list. Municipal logistics base was formed, an LPA platoon of 40 conscripts was established, three district staffs were formed, and to avoid wasting time, you have seen this document, the regional -- the district staff of TO Potocari was established, the TO Suceska, TO Osatica and a communications or liaison platoon was formed. My question is: On the 15th of April 1992, you were working in the Secretariat for All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this sort of decision?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This decision was made while the Serbs were still in Srebrenica, and I think it was the last day, when the administrative organ of Srebrenica municipality was working.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this decision ever implemented to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It could never be implemented because as soon as the 16th of April 1992, the municipality stopped working. It was no longer possible to work because people were leaving Srebrenica, even Nurija who was the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence left for Tuzla between the 15th and the 16th of April, and Suljo Hasanovic also left Srebrenica. He went to Suceska and he actually hailed from Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to work in those days?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Only on the following day, the 16th. My husband and I -- because my husband was also working in the municipal administrative organ and to my surprise, when I arrived there, I saw only the potter locking up the building. He was surprised when he saw me. He said, "Haven't you left yet?" I said, "Why?" And he said, "Madam, war has broken out." And I remember well the porter's name was Srecko. I have forgotten his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on to the next question, could this document be given a Defence Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can I have the sequence? D-1001.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you left your home?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the 17th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where you went?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: When the shelling started on the 17th of April 1992, I was confused. I couldn't believe it, I didn't know what was going on. The shelling was so intense, even around my house, and I had small children. We tried to leave but we couldn't go to Bratunac because they were already coming from Bratunac towards Srebrenica, the Serbs, I mean, so then we tried to go to a Muslim village in the direction of Bajina Basta, towards Osat. In order to reach those villages, we had to go through a Serb village called Pribicevac. There we had a friend with whom we had socialised. I used to buy cheese from them and cream. He would use our telephone when he needed because they didn't have telephone lines in the village. When we came to his house, he took us in, but he was so afraid, he and his wife. I had two young children and she only looked at the children and she spoke to the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these Serbs, Madam?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Serb. His first name was Srecko. I don't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, you said that this was in the village of Pribicevac. Did you see any military presence in the village of Pribicevac or not?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That was the reason why we did not move ahead. That was the reason why we went to Mr. Srecko's. We wanted to ask him about the goings on in the area since we had seen a large military presence in Zalazje, Brezani. They were positioning mortars in between houses. It was horrific. This was my first encounter and experience with weaponry and uniformed persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the army Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: This was a Serb army that was preparing an attack against Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in this Serb house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Not very long. First of all we waited for the darkness to set in and then we asked Srecko's son to escort us through the area over to the free territory, to try and circumvent the lines where they had already positions mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any other artillery there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Whether we were on our way, Srecko asked us to avoid these spots although I wanted to see for myself. I was sorry to leave the area. Mr. Srecko is a wonderful plan. He did whatever he could to help us to escort us through the woods to the liberated territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Madam. I asked you whether you had seen any other artillery pieces. You said you did but nothing further was recorded.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were mortars that were positioned between houses. They were small-calibre artillery because they were not very far from Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you mention a tank as well?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a tank going from Brezani through Zalazje in the direction of Sase. This was the only road they could have taken. It was also the road that provided the best view of Srebrenica for shelling purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When -- where did you go when you left the house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: In the woods above Guber. There is a large wooded area near to Guber. We met up with a large group of our neighbours, people who were retreating. These were people who remained in Srebrenica because they had not left earlier. They also retreated into the woods and they told us not to go into the town that it was very dangerous there, that the Serbs had already entered the town, and that they were killing everything that moved, and that they were torching houses and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the woods with your children?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: For about two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any accommodation there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were staying outdoors. The only shelter we had were the trees. It was November -- it was April. There was rain, even snow. It was very difficult. We had to make some makeshift shelter for the children to sleep under, like spreading nylons, and there was many families with children there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: After the death of Goran Zekic but we waited two more days after his death because we weren't sure whether they had already withdrawn from the town or not. When Zekic died the Serb army withdrew from Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In June and July 1992, you were in Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what the situation in Srebrenica was like? Was it peaceful or were there some war operations on?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Ever since or rather from April 1992 through to July 1995, there was not a moment of peace in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was Srebrenica shelled in June and July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: It was in May, June, July and August, through to the demilitarisation that the shelling was very intense. They were shelling all the time. Even when there was a lull in shelling you never knew when the shelling was going to resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there people coming into town who were not from Srebrenica? Can you tell the Trial Chamber in fact how many Srebrenica residents stayed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Out of 6.000 to 7.000 Srebrenica inhabitants only some 300 stayed behind, that's together, men, women and children. All the others fled from Srebrenica in April 1992. Most of them left on the 14th, 15th, and 16th of April, even at night, on buses, to Tuzla, to Bajina Basta, wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Some 300 native Srebrenica residents stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were people who hailed from Srebrenica and resided there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did other people start coming in?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Already in May, the first refugees from Bratunac started arriving because it was at the time that the Serbs entered Bratunac, drove the people away and looted the town. As Bratunac is the neighbouring municipality to Srebrenica, they fled to the wooded areas just as we did initially and then went on to Srebrenica. Most of them were women and children. They were -- they lacked clothing and footwear. They were naked, practically.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there others arriving from other towns?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In July-August there were people arriving from Zvornik, Visegrad, Rogatica, Han Pijesak, although most of them were from Bratunac. Others arrived from Zepa as well, whenever they felt that the danger there was greater than in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your return to Srebrenica, were you able to see whether the public institutions in the town had been looted?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They looted the public institutions and companies first. I experienced this myself. I saw it for myself. Guber is positioned on higher ground compared to the town itself. I was at Guber and I was able to see trucks arriving in the morning from the direction of Bajina Basta and Zalazje. They first looted Arbin Kari [phoen] which is an outdoor spa. They proceeded to loot hotel Domavija, the Drina managing board, the mining managing board, other businesses, then the municipal building, the court, and lastly the hospital as well. We were able to see them taking items out and loading them on to a truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the intellectuals of Srebrenica who used to live there before the war stay behind?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Few of them remained but most of them fled in 1992, as I've already said, on the 14th, 15th or the 16th of April. The Serbs and the Muslims were supposed to meet in Bratunac. I believe it was supposed to take place on the 14th of April 1992. Dr. Sabit Begic attended the meeting, where they were supposed to find a peaceful solution and coexistence for the people in the area. When he returned from the meeting he was very disappointed. He was telling people to leave, that peace could not be preserved. I saw a list that he held which contained the names of all the intellectuals that were supposed to be liquidated, killed. I was there among other people who were curious to know what was going on, and I asked him, "What are you talking about?" He replied, "You heard what I said. Tell your husband not to stay behind. You should leave. You should not stay. Bad things are going to happen."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When Dr. Begic was talking about a list, was it a list containing the names of Muslim intellectuals or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim intellectuals, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us who was it that remained in Srebrenica? What was the makeup of the people who stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: These were ordinary people. Some of them were educated but most weren't because most of the educated ones had left. So these were the people who stayed behind, whereas those families who were better off had left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said families who were better off. You said Serb families, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These were Serb families, decent Serb families who did not want to have anything to do with the others who stayed behind and were later involved in the looting and other such activities. But such decent families were very few.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Dzemal Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How well did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirevic was deputy of Mr. Nedzad Selmanagic, who was deputy chief for business. Since Selmanagic had fled Srebrenica at the very start, he went to his native village. He returned to Srebrenica town at the same time we did, when we returned from the woods, and he tried to do his best to make the economy operational. However, he was unable to do much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of July 1992, did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I had been working there before the war, and there were not many people left who used to work there, he invited me to work with him, to help the people arriving who had no where to stay, had nothing to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go and work in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: In late July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you came there, were there other people already working there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was this municipal War Presidency, the members of which were already there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when they were elected? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I learned that from Mr. Becirevic. It was from the 1st of July 1992 that the War Presidency was operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you come to know whether the War Presidency, ever since its inception in early July 1992, had been seated in the municipal building or not?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were seated in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until when?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Until the offices in the municipal building were refurbished, because the building had been looted, the window panes had been shattered, and they had to scrape and find pieces of furniture, office equipment, in order to move the offices to the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many office rooms had been made usable by the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, some five or six of them were made fit to be worked in, although it was all improvised.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where these rooms were located?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had two office rooms on the ground floor, in the municipal building, and three or possibly four on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was based in the offices on the ground floor and who was based on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Mevludin Becirevic was in one of the rooms, and in the other room, there was the head of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where were those two rooms?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: They were on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the other ones?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: On the second floor where the president of the municipal War Presidency, Hajrudin Abdic, was located, the president of the executive board, Hamdija Fejzic, occupied the other room and the third room was occupied by Mustafa Sacirovic aka Mule, in the office that was next to the Office of the President of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, could you please repeat the name of the person in charge of the civilian protection? Because the interpreter did not manage to catch the name?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Jusuf Halilovic. He occupied the same position before the war as well, that is to say chief of the civilian protection, and he tried to continue discharging his duties although in very improvised conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that the offices were put together in an improvised manner, that they had to obtain pieces of furniture from different places. Did you have typewriters, mechanical typewriters or any other pieces of equipment that you needed for your work?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had two very old mechanical typewriters, but we lacked inked ribbons, paper. We had only one ribbon. So we lacked stationery; the equipment itself means nothing unless you have the attendant stationery.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the office stationery that was in stock?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember. The entire office equipment and stationery was taken away by the Serbs at the time when they were looting the building. This included paper, electrical typewriters, none of those were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will put a simple question to you now. Before demilitarisation in Srebrenica, did you have occasion to see a single document produced on high-quality imported paper?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. We lacked ordinary paper, let alone that sort of paper. We never had that sort of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of paper did you use?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever we were able to find some paper after rummaging the cabinets there, we would use paper that had already been used on one side, for instance take a sheet of paper. If one side had already been used we would use the other side whenever we needed it urgently.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the paper situation, did it change considerably after the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, it remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive some paper in, for instance, the court?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: We did receive some thin sort of paper in limited quantities after the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what the situation was like in the library and what happened to papers such as regulations in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Little of that remained. They looted and took everything with them. Whatever was left behind, the refugees who were coming to town would rummage the cabinets in search of paper for cigarettes. You know that people did not have any proper tobacco, they would use plants, dry different plants, and then rummage the cabinets for paper. I even saw people taking books from the town library. There were thousands of people around in the streets before accommodation was found for them. It was very difficult to find accommodation for them. When there was no more space in private homes, the refugees who were subsequently arriving had to be found makeshift accommodation in different warehouses and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have I understood what you said, they were using this paper also as fuel for fire to keep themselves warm?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because there was no firewood, there was no heating, there was no water.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Becirevic called you to the municipality and asked you to work there. Did you work with him or were you given other tasks?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I worked with Mr. Becirevic for only a brief time because there was nothing for him to do. When they saw that the economy could not be started up again, that everything had been looted, then Hamdija, Dzemo Becirevic, and the president of the War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic, agreed that I should go and work for him in the municipal War Presidency, that I would be there with him and work there because I was familiar with administrative procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the job you started to do?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Technical secretary. This was all makeshift, improvised. There were no proper conditions to work but we did our best.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness be shown Exhibit D986?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the document. During our proofing session I showed you this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to ask you, when you arrived there, did Mr. Avdic, or did he not, tell you who the members of the War Presidency were?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you who his associates were?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived there -- please take a look at the list. Were these people members of the War Presidency? I will read the names out to you. Avdic, Hajrudin?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hamdija Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Next to his name, we have -- it says chairman of the IO?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: That was the executive committee which was part of the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you got there, was Mr. Fejzic introduced to you as the chairman of the executive committee?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dzemal Becirevic, is that the person you've been mentioning?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Dzemaludin but people called him Dzemo, Dzjemo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: And he was the chief of the economy.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Resid Efendic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the secretary of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Jusuf Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, he was the civilian protection chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Becir Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the chief of the public security station. That was its name then, or secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Adziz Nekic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were deputies but they were also members of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mirsad Dudic, Sefik Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, him as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And here we have the name of Mirzet Halilovic, military police commander?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know he was a military police commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The people on this list, were they in the War Presidency all the time, all of them? Take a look at the list.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not all of them. Some of them were but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was there all the time or very often?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Those who were there all the time were the president of the War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic, and the chairman of the executive committee, Hamdija Fejzic, Dzemal Becirevic also, who was in charge of the economy, Resid Efendic, the secretary of the municipal War Presidency, and Jusuf Halilovic and Becir Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nekic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nekic was there as well because he sat with Dzemal Becirevic in the same office.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Naser, Dudic, and Mandzic, how often did they come there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Rarely. They attended meetings very rarely. They only dropped in from time to time and they rarely attended meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how often Naser attended meetings in person and how often he came to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He came very rarely, perhaps once a week or maybe even once a month, up to December 1992. I heard about Naser when I started working but it was a long time before I met him. I met him or rather I just saw him and I asked people who he was because he came in so rarely. When I first saw him, I was expecting to see him because Naser was a very nice young man. He was almost a child. So that when he came in, I would just look at him. He was a real child. He was so young.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you something else about this. To the best of your knowledge, after October 1992, was he a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. He was no longer a member of the War Presidency and from October until the demilitarisation, I never saw him again in the municipality, at least I didn't see him, and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now is perhaps a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. We will have a 30-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown a video clip? This is Exhibit P328, tape 4, from 004505 to 004557.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 4757, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "... instructions no longer able to apply. [inaudible]. All the commanders of the various Territorial Defence units all became commanders of the War Presidency. [inaudible]. So now we have to [inaudible]. Sefik Mandzic and his units had managed to connect with these various enclaves. [inaudible] included him as well as a member of the War Presidency. [inaudible] included the lads from the area of Osmace [inaudible] War Presidency too. They wanted to be their own separate entity within the [inaudible] Territorial Defence and they have one of their members in the War Presidency. That village now had [inaudible] Under them. This was [inaudible] a military power. [inaudible] completed military academy. Bektic. Nedzad Bektic. His name was Nedzad Bektic, that's N-e-d -- sorry, N-e-d [inaudible] a-r, and then Bektic, B-e-k-t-i-c. [inaudible]."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you heard this part of the interview more than once during our proofing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that Mr. Oric says -- well, first of all, let me tell you, do you recognise the person who is speaking as Naser?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you notice that he says that all the Territorial Defence commanders together with him became members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard him say that but that's not true, because the local group leaders, only two of them, and later a third, became a member of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who were these two?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Dudic and Mandzic, Sefik Mandzic and Mirsad Dudic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the third one you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, it was Senahid Tabakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just because some problems with the English, the video would say all the commanders from the various Territorial Defence units all became commanders of the War Presidency, did not speak of members of the War Presidency. But it did not speak members of the War Presidency, but of commanders of the War Presidency, whereas later on you asked whether they became members of the War Presidency. So there is a difference between commanders of the War Presidency that was translated from the video and your question where you speak of members. So could you perhaps clarify the difference?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what the person who said Oric -- who was speaking, Oric said was members. We will very soon address the Court with a submission as regards the interview. This is something I perhaps shouldn't say right now but very often, you will come across misinterpretations and that's a problem. However, what both the witness and I heard was that he was speaking of members of the War Presidency, and I'm basing my questions on what we heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear that he was speaking of members of the War Presidency and commanders of the territorial units?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The other members of the War Presidency, were they, as Naser says here, commanders of the Territorial Defences, Efendic, Halilovic, Bogilovic, Avdic, Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, none of them were. None of them was a local group leader. We only had local group leaders there. We had no commanders and no army. Let's understand one another. Had we had an army, believe me, what happened would not have happened. We only had groups of people defending Srebrenica and they had their own local group leaders. I never saw any army there. Had we had an army, probably what happened would not have happened. Everybody knows what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Nedzad Bektic a member of the War Presidency, ever?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The information provided by Oric here, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know what Mr. Oric was saying. I listened to it but it's unclear. He was probably misinformed, because he wasn't -- or, rather, he was rarely there. He rarely attended meetings of the War Presidency. He was always at the line. He was always in boots. And perhaps he was misinformed. I don't know where he got the information from.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These local group leaders, did they occasionally come to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Some of them did, yes, from time to time, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether any of the local group leaders dropped in more often than others?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember Zulfo Tursunovic, also known as Cica, he would come to the municipality quite often to see the president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a reason? Could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avdic was a man who rarely had someone close to him, but Zulfo Tursunovic was close to him and they would often talk. But this was mainly about refugees, their accommodation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a reason why Zulfo Tursunovic was close to Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: They came from the same village, Suceska. That was the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long had you worked with Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: From late July, early August, up until the setting up of the lower court in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which year did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the municipal court in Srebrenica was established?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: It was established sometime in May 1993, but it did not start operating proceeding right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will get back to that at a later stage. I have something else to ask you now. Do you want to tell us that you knew Mr. Hajrudin Avdic well?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I worked with him. I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, was he the sort of personality who would be a pushover, who would -- who could have other views imposed on him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, far from that. He was a man of authority and influence, quite an educated man. He was an electrical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P14? For the record, this is allegedly the decision of the armed forces of Srebrenica dated 22 December 1992. I will quote the decision. "The -- pursuant to the conclusions reached at the meeting of the Srebrenica OS staff on 22nd December 1992 the commander of the Srebrenica armed forces issues the following order. A meeting of the War Presidency and the Srebrenica OS staff is to be held on the 23rd of December 1992 at 1000 hours. The president of the War Presidency is hereby obliged to ensure the quorum before the start of the meeting."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you were working in the War Presidency in this particular period of time, in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this document before your coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at the document now? Does the document show that it had been received by the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, because had it been received, the document should have in the upper left-hand corner, "Delivered to" at such and such a time to such and such a person. Since it does not contain this it shows nothing of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were working as a technical secretary in the Presidency. Would such document end up in your hands?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Whatever was sent to us first came to me and then I would forward the documentation to Hajrudin Avdic, the president of the War Presidency of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you worked there, did you ever receive a document wherein Naser was ordering something to Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I don't think that Mr. Naser Oric was ever able to issue any orders to Mr. Hajrudin Avdic because Mr. Hajrudin Avdic was the president of the municipal War Presidency and was his superior, as well as the superior of all the others working in the different institutions. It was all improvised.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Naser ever scheduled any meetings of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. The president of the municipal War Presidency, that's to say Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, scheduled meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know on what terms Mr. Naser Oric and Mr. Avdic were? Was it -- were these relations correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were correct. They cooperated as far as they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you had occasion to see that Naser Oric attended several meetings of the War Presidency or that he came to the building of the War Presidency. Can you tell us what sort of a personality did he display? Was he an imposing person?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. He would just drop by briefly to discuss certain matters and then leave. He is such a sensitive person, he was young and quite handsome at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a person who would impose himself on others,?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Everybody liked Naser, including the children. Children wanted to style themselves after him, to have the same hair style and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- why did they in fact like him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever he was passing in the street, people, including the children, admired him. He was a sort of idol to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why is that? Was there some specific event that triggered this?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the month of April of 1992, there was a group of Arkan's men who wanted to make an incursion into the town, and Naser managed to foil this action of theirs and to prevent them from massacring the people in the town, and I believe this is what was the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown another video clip, part of P318, to stop at 000538?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, do you recognise anyone here on this still?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Only the lad in uniform in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the one to whom the arrow is pointing?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's the young man who is in centre left of the still wearing a uniform. Can you tell the Trial Chamber who that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: His name is Hazim. He was a refugee from Voljavica, from the Bratunac area. He lived in my neighbourhood as a refugee. He was accommodated in a house near to where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he resemble someone?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He resembled Naser. He tried to imitate him, you know. Before I got to know Naser well, I always winced at seeing him because I thought it was him. Many people thought that he was Naser, and vice versa. They would confuse the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to Hajrudin Avdic now. Mr. Hajrudin Avdic and the War Presidency, did it try in any way to introduce law and order in the town?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Hajrudin Avdic and all the other members of the War Presidency tried to introduce law and order not only in Srebrenica town but in the entire Srebrenica area. You know what the situation was like. We were isolated. We didn't have any electricity, running water, no communications with the outside world. We had no food, no fuel for heating, no clothing. On the other side, we had many refugees, first those from Bratunac, then as I said from Vlasenica, Rogatica, part of Han Pijesak, Zvornik, Rogatica and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was he trying to do? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: First of all he tried to introduce peace to the town. Many were expelled, lost family members, had no accommodation, spent days in the streets. There was general dissatisfaction and somebody had to be present to explain to them, to be patient, to try and find accommodation and food for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was he ever successful in his attempts to do these things in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. He wasn't. It was impossible, despite his endeavours, the situation was horrific, terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he try to keep the people who were coming into town under control in some way?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was trying to do that through the police force. Often times he would call Becir Bogilovic, who was chief of the police, to discuss ways in which peace could be restored.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he try to have lists made of persons coming to town and leaving the town, to keep a record of the sort?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were attempts at that but it was impossible because whenever people came to town and realised that there was no food or accommodation, they would go back to the villages in the free territory -- on the free territory. They would go to -- back to the countryside where there was land to be farmed and some food to be had.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to mean that there was a constant flux of people moving to and fro?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
