utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At one point we had about 30.000 refugees in such a confined area, and these people were constantly on the move, going into the countryside and back into town. I apologise. They would do so whenever the circumstances permitted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have another question in connection with this. Was there some sort of a pass required in order to enter Srebrenica or some other sort of document?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was far from possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone entering Srebrenica with some sort of a pass?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Hajrudin Avdic and War Presidency have accurate information about what was happening in the entire general area?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not possible. We did not have any sort of communication. The only source of communication were people who -- or rather source of information were people, refugees who would come to town or the wounded victims of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there an organised courier system?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It could not have existed because people could not move. Nobody would risk their lives to do that sort of job.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that in spite of that some persons tried to do the job and got killed in the process?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact that was why it was difficult to organise the police service. People who would be moving through the town and into the countryside would get killed very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, were -- was there disinformation spread around in the course of 1992 through to the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very often refugees coming from the countryside would tell us that this or that particular village had been captured, fallen, this and that person had been killed, and then at the end of the day, one would find out that this was an untruth, this was a lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like in Srebrenica in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: It was already quite chaotic. Many refugees, most of whom had no accommodation or food, diseases were thriving. The hospital was unable to function. We did not have food or medicines.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, was Srebrenica isolated?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Srebrenica was in isolation from April 1992 through to the 12th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in the summer of 1992, was there some sort of communication established with the outside world in spite of that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was only the information line.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: These were amateur radio operators. It was them who operated this communications line.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: In the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who headed this particular service?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. If you can just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that these were ham radio operators and that there was this service in the municipal -- in the municipal organ. Do you recall who headed the service?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. If I can have some time to try and recollect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can get back to that later. Do you recall who worked there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do. I know that Ibrahim Becirevic worked there, with two lads, twins, from Bratunac. Their last name was Dautbasic. I can't recall their first names.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This service, was it part of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The service was part of the War Presidency, as were all the other institutions in the municipality. All the municipal institutions were under the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name of Alic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Alic was the chief of the service and member of the War Presidency. I recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean part of War Presidency or member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Member of the War Presidency but the entire service was part of--

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Part of what?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Part of the war -- municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that there were amateur radio operators there. Was anybody allowed to just go over there and use the equipment?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. This would be impossible. There were many refugees, all of whom wanted to get in touch with their family outside. And this was the only line through which they were able to get in touch with theirs, with fair families, so there was a decision in place that all those who wanted to use the equipment had to first approach the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, who would then issue them with a permit or a certificate of a sort enabling them to get in touch with their family.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it always Mr. Avdic issuing these certificates? What happened in his absence?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Hamdija Fejzic would do that in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your earlier testimony you told us that on the second floor of the municipal building near to the office of the president of the War Presidency, Mustafa Sacir had his office. Do you remember what his duty was?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He ran a service in charge of collecting information on the war crimes and damages, war damages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he worked on his own or whether he worked with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He had two associates, Sabahudin Gluhic and Edhem Vranjkovina also known as Gedjo. They filmed together and collected the information together. He was their boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were independent or part of another service?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: They were part of the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were they part of the information service or not?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were part of the information service. They cooperated with them, brought the materials after they had filmed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness two exhibits, two Defence Exhibits, simultaneously D266 and D865?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at D266 first. This is an order issued by the municipal War Presidency of Srebrenica dated the 16th of August 1992. It seems to have been signed by Mr. Avdic. And then please look at document D865, also an order signed by someone. Do you remember these documents? Did you see them before your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I typed out this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The typewritten one?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I typed it out and gave it to Edhem Vranjkovina and Gluhic, Sabahudin myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this signature as somebody's signature?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the signature of president of the municipal War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now please look at this other document, D865. It's also an order but it's handwritten. Whose handwriting is this, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the handwriting of the president of the municipal War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic. Whenever I wasn't there, he would write orders by hand and give them to Edhem Vranjkovina or Sabahudin Gluhic or Edhem Sacirovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Murat Efendic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his role was during the war?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was a member of the municipal War Presidency, but he was in Sarajevo, not in Srebrenica. He fled in 1992, as did many others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone had contacts with him from Srebrenica, from July or August 1992 or the summer of 1992, until the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Hajrudin Avdic had contacts with him through the information service, through the ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how this was done? What sort of contacts were these? What was this about?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: These were mostly appeals for help and various reports. We would report on the situation on the ground, on the free territory of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown D575, a document issued by the Srebrenica War Presidency dated the 6th of April 1993? It's entitled, "Statement."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at this document. Do you agree that there is a -- the heading of the War Presidency of Srebrenica and that below the text, to the left, it says, received by ham radio, and then there is a mark and it says, received by Ilijaz Omerovic, and to the right it says War Presidency, Srebrenica municipality, and something that looks like M Efendic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the manner of communication that you described when you said that the War Presidency communicated through the information service with its representative in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is how communications took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with this I want to ask you the following. How was this information generated, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: People would come from the ground, and from the free territories. People who had been expelled would come to the town, and they would first come to the municipal building to ask for assistance, and to say that there were wounded people out there, that it was difficult to bring them in, that the situation was terrible, that civilians were getting killed. There was nothing we could do to help them because we had no means at our disposal, and then we would send out these appeals and reports asking Sarajevo Tuzla and the international community to assist us. The only source were ham radio operators and these communiques and appeals and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Technically, how was this generated? Did you type it out? Did Mr. Avdic dictate this to someone? Technically, how was it done?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I would type out a report or an appeal and sometimes Mr. Avdic himself would go to the post office where the ham radio operators were and he would dictate to them directly, it would all depend on the situation, because I wasn't always there when there was heavy shelling, very often I couldn't leave my house, I couldn't reach the municipal building from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness document D417, D417. The ERN number is 01787880, and this is information from the information service of the War Presidency dated the 11th of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this document?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the information service of the War Presidency? Is this the same service?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same service, though the War Presidency had offices in the municipal building and the information service in the post office.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this service, was there any other similar service in Srebrenica, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: The question isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I meant to ask: Was there another information service apart from the municipal information service?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was the only information service and the only means of communication were the ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, please look at this document and I will read out a part to you, which says -- it's around the middle of the first paragraph, and it says, "Concentration of the army has been observed probably the Uzice and Valjevo corps. To date in the last two months 30 people have been killed including 12 children in the area, about 70 people have been wounded, hundreds of facilities have been destroyed, all religious and school facilities have been almost entirely destroyed, not a single residential building is undamaged. And what is worse, people cannot survive in the camps in the woods. With the excuse that the hydroelectric power plant is being secured against the Green Berets, the Yugoslav military hordes shell this area daily. The population of this area has been left to these criminals as game to be hunted down." Do you remember seeing this document before?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I typed it out. I was so terrified while I was typing it out that I made a lot of mistakes. What was important was, regardless of grammatical errors and so on, to get this information through. I was trying to do this as quickly as possible because shells were landing close to the municipal building, and I was terrified while I was typing this out. We really needed assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember to whom you gave it?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I gave it to Mr. Alic. Mr. Alic was waiting for me to finish typing it out to hand it to him so that he could send it. I remember him telling me there is no heading, and I said, "Sir, put it there yourself. You can see what a hurry I'm in. I'm afraid for my life and you're talking about a heading."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how was this information obtained, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: From people who brought the wounded into hospital, people who arrived in town, people who were fleeing from their homes. They all came to town and they had all heard that there was a municipal War Presidency who might be able to help them. The corridors were full. I recall this very well. The building was full of children.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll show you another document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown document RR321924. This is a document bearing the heading, "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Srebrenica municipality War Presidency." The date is the 9th of November 1992, and the title is, "Decision on appointment." I will quote to you what it says. It says "Asim Djozic from Srebrenica is hereby appointed as the member of the executive board in the field of agriculture and forestry. Osman Suljic from Srebrenica is hereby appointed as a member of the executive board in the field of industry and mining. Avdo Hasanovic from Srebrenica is hereby appointed as the member of the executive board in the field of health and social welfare. Nesib Mandzic from Srebrenica is hereby appointed as a member of the executive board in the field of education and information. Abdurahman Malkic from Poznanovic is hereby appointed as the member of the executive board in the field of transport and communications. Aziz Mujic is hereby appointed as the secretary of the executive board," and it says, "No decision shall enter into force on the day of issuing." The signature seems to be that of Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. First of all I want to ask you whether you saw this decision before I showed it to you on your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because I typed it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What body was this executive board part of?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: It was part of the service of the municipal War Presidency and initially there was only the chairperson of the executive board. It was only on the 9th of November that the decision on appointment was issued appointing these members of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- I will now ask you to think about Mr. Hamdija Fejzic a little bit. What was he by profession?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He was an economist. He had graduated from the faculty of economics at the university.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you say that Mr. Fejzic in your view it was an educated man?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was very literate. He had a university education. Of course he had to be both literate and educated.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to work with him? Did you see him write something? Did you ever type for him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I was there on my own to begin with, what I'm trying to say is that in 1992, I was the only one working with Mr. Hamdija Fejzic and the president of the municipal War Presidency, Mr. Avdic. As we were all on the same floor I would work for both of them. Whenever they had something.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he make grammar mistakes when speaking or writing?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He was a really educated man. And he was a very decent sort of person.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were the members of the executive board members of the War Presidency ex officio?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the executive board was part of the municipal War Presidency, of course, they were members.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were they members or did they work in the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were not members but they worked in the War Presidency. I do apologise. The question wasn't clear to me, because this Asim Djozic, I don't know him at all. He was but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the name --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: The name Avdo Hasanovic was a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please let's dwell on Avdo Hasanovic for a while. Is this the same person as Dr. Avdo Hasanovic who had something to do with the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the director of the hospital in Srebrenica during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you arrived in late July 1992. From when did Dr. Avdo Hasanovic start coming to the War Presidency, if he did at all?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: When I started working, I noticed Avdo Hasanovic right away. He often came to see Mr. Avdic. If someone was with Mr. Avdic he would wait in my office and he would talk about the problems and I was familiar with that, about the problems in the hospital, they didn't have enough food, bedding, medicines, bandages, heating fuel. We had no electricity, no water. Communications were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the form of this decision. Look at it well. Above the title is the heading and to the right is something that's handwritten. You told us that you typed this out. What does this handwritten bit mean to you?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It doesn't mean anything to me. It wasn't there when I was typing it. All that was there was the typed part and what it says here at the bottom, submitted to and so on. When I typed out a document, it had to be a complete document. I would never have omitted to say, "Submitted to," for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you're mentioning this "submitted to", let's clarify this. On the right-hand side, at the bottom, is the signature and on the left-hand side at the bottom it says, "Submitted to the above-named and the archives." Let me ask you now: As I understand it, throughout your life, both before, during, and after the war, you worked in state organs, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, was it usual or not to include in documents all those to whom the document is submitted?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would make the document valid. Without it, it would mean nothing. It would be only a draft document or an incomplete text.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If a decision were to be made only for the purposes of the archives, would this be designated accordingly?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it would. It would say, "To be delivered to the archives, the files." For short, "A-A."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If someone were to dictate one such decision to you, without telling you to whom the decision should be delivered, could this decision subsequently be acted upon?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It would, to me it would mean that it was just a draft of a decision that could not be acted upon and could not be forwarded to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document be assigned an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, Madam Vidovic will become Defence Exhibit D1002.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown a video clip, which is Prosecution Exhibit P317. The video is 3939, one of two. Could the video be played from 000549 to 000559, and to stop at 005509.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who this is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you play the clip on and stop at 00060632?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can see some people there. Do you know who these people are?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I can't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen them?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I only saw them that day when I brought them into this room.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as to who these people were?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: These were people who came from Tuzla with Dr. Nedret, and this was summer 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we proceed with the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. I recognise Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest that Defence counsel could ask Ms. Djilovic to say which people is she referring to that she doesn't know. From our screen, they are very -- as a matter of fact, it's very difficult to see. I see two dark figures, and there was one person with blond hair. Is she referring to those three? Because now she's talked about she didn't recognise them but then she brought them in. But there is also another person there who is in a white shirt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's fair enough. Let's go back and review the video and just try to take into account what has been pointed out by Ms. Sellers and repeat the question or at least indicate to the witness the persons you are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about the persons one can see at 0632?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thee two persons one can see in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the record, one switches on the computer evidence mode, we have a still at 0632, which shows just two persons, both male, and the witness is being directed to these two persons. Do you want to, for the time being, ask the witness a question, a specific question, in relation to these two persons? Then if you are interested in other persons we'll move forward with the video and you put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would also like the witness to see the blond person and to ask her whether she knows the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment before we move any further. Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: The witness had mentioned that they had brought in certain persons, so before we go on, I would like to ask whether she also had brought in the two people in uniform which we had seen on the screen so far. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So when you say yes, does it mean that you also had brought in these two persons in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only escorted them into the office. I'll explain this to you later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you very much, Judge Eser. Madam Vidovic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this person in the company of these young men you escorted? Were they together?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were together.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please play the video and stop at 000636?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you in connection with this is as follows: Is it true that you viewed this footage with me several times during proofing?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the room?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the room of the executive committee of the municipal War Presidency where Hamdija Fejzic as the president of the executive committee worked. That's his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play the video please and stop at 000725?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise these people?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know the young man in uniform and the lady with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber who these people are?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Halilovic and the lady's first name is Ajka. I don't know her family name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the whole situation and why these people were there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Avdic was absent that day. Hamdija Fejzic, the president of the executive committee, stood for him. And all these people arrived there with the same purpose, asking for permission to get in touch with their family members with the help of the ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who this lady came with?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: With Mirzet Halilovic. I believe that the man filming the footage was with them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the first name of the Halilovic that you identified here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mirzet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Naser come together with them or on his own or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naser Oric came on his own. He asked for Hamdija Fejzic. I asked him to step in and to wait for Mr. Fejzic. In the meantime others arrived including those young men from Tuzla who told me that they had come with Nedret and that they would like to get in touch with their family, probably in Tuzla or somewhere else, and I escorted them into Hamdija Fejzic's office as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who filmed this?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. It was a young man who was together with this lady and I don't think anyone of -- anyone was there on official business.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I -- do you recall seeing here in this footage a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. There is an outdated mechanical typewriter that was left behind. This is one of the two typewriters we had in the municipality. It lacked the ribbon which meant that practically one couldn't use it. There was another such a type writer that was in my office and I used it to the extent we had to use it because we only had that one ribbon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now put questions to you in relation to the War Presidency itself. Do you recall the way the Presidency functioned?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did they in fact do or what did they try to do?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the War Presidency tried to restore law and order, first of all, to make the police force operational, as well as the hospital, to collect food on the free territory and across the territory for the hospital, for the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the War Presidency try to organise mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were such attempts but they were never successful. It was impossible. Besides, there was no need for that. People volunteered themselves to protect their own families. So there was no point really.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What makes you think that they failed to organise mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the fact that they had no access to refugees?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: When you want to mobilise a person you have to have conditions in place. If you want to send the person to the front line you have to have food, clothing, footwear and, of course, weapons. We had none of that and we were unable to mobilise people without these things. Nobody could order people to go to the front line, not even Mr. Avdic, because the persons first concern was in that case you have to provide my family with food, you have to provide me with clothing, footwear, weapons. We had none of that. We were isolated and we had many, many refugees, the town and the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come to know that there were weapons but they were in possession of the people who refused to fight, to become fighters?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever a person got hold of a piece of weapon, they would keep the weapon for themselves, for their own protection when they went in search of food, when they went through villages in search of corn and so on and so forth, they concealed the weapons because they wanted to keep the weapons for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the War Presidency try to do something about these weapons?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, I heard Mr. Avdic calling Bogilovic and telling him to work on his police officers, to try and do something about it. However, this wasn't a true police force. They had no uniforms or weapons. He'd plead with them to go around and -- in search of weapons but it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the War Presidency have meetings before demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did. But rarely. Maybe once or twice a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why were these meetings held rarely?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the general situation in the town and in the free territory. There was unabated shelling. It was unsafe to move around. During shelling, the priorities were the municipal building, the hospital and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the persons present at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. These were members of the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did local group leaders attend on some occasions?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did on some occasions but quite rarely. The conditions did not permit them to move around or to leave the front lines. They were under continuous attack and they could not afford to lose the areas of territory that were still free.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself personally sit out these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not. It was only on some occasions when Mr. Avdic asked me to write some reports about what had been discussed at the meeting that I would attend to make it easier for me to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what your precise duties were as a technical secretary?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: My duty was to follow the work and to assist Mr. Avdic in his work. If two or three parties came to see him all at once, I would make sure who would go in first, who would stay behind. Then I would type out whatever was necessary. But we mostly typed out appeals for help.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a technical secretary, were you aware of who was coming to see Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whoever came to see Mr. Avdic had to go through my office. I had to announce their visit and only then could they be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the reasons which prompted the persons to see Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Not always but for the most part I did because the people themselves would tell me. Normally, if the chief of police came, it was for some sort of a problem. If Mr. Avdo came from the health centre or manager Hasanovic from the hospital, the motives were that they needed food or medicines, and I believe I've already mentioned all the items that were needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the absence of Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, did you receive messages that were for him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would relay to him whatever verbal or written messages were left for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see the messages that came from Mr. Efendic through the ham radio operators?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because for the most part I would be receiving those messages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hamed Alic frequently have contact was Mr. Avdic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did it daily. This was a gentleman who was the chief of communications. He worked with a ham radio operators. He worked in the information service. He would often drop in. He would bring in an appeal or a report and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mustafa Sacirovic known as Mule come to see him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mustafa came on a daily basis. Almost every morning he would come to meet him and tell him about the situation, what they had seen. He would bring him the films and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who Mr. Hajrudin Avdic's associates were?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was there and I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bogilovic come to see Mr. Hajrudin Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Very often. For a while, he didn't come, when he was wounded, but then afterwards he came again, and I remember he used a stick when he walked. I remember him with his stick. He never really recovered. In 1993 he didn't leave because his wound never healed properly. He was unable to treat it properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he arrived on his own or with someone? I'm talking about the period before December 1992, Madam.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He would usually come in with Mirzet Halilovic or very often with Nurija Jusufovic. I remember his name now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have meetings with Mr. Avdic, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I now wish to ask you, to the best of your recollection, did Nurija Jusufovic come to see Mr. Avdic on his own as well?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, often, usually when there were problems. Nurija Jusufovic was a commander of the civilian police. Let's call it a police force although it was not a proper police force because they didn't have uniforms or weapons or any kind of working conditions, but they did try.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mirzet Halilovic come to see Mr. Avdic on his own? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did it happen often or rarely?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: You could say that he came quite often. Hajrudin would often ask him to come and see him. He even criticised him on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, to the best of your knowledge, what did Mirzet Halilovic do? What was his task?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He was a kind of commander of some sort of military police. I think it existed only on paper, because to have a military police and not have an army, that's ridiculous, really. Attempts were being made to introduce law and order, so there was the civilian police and the military police, but they all worked together. They shared premises and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see who Mirzet Halilovic's superior was?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Becir Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the basis for your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever there was a problem, Hajrudin would call Becir and say, Why do you allow this and why do you allow that? I wasn't there but I could hear them through the wall because it was a very thin wall, a very thin partition dividing his office from mine and he would raise his voice and when he raised his voice I would hear what he was saying. And he would complain that there was nothing he could do about him, that he was a man who did what he liked, especially when he got a bit drunk.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify, Madam, who was complaining about whom?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic was complaining to Hajrudin about Mirzet Halilovic, saying that he was insubordinate, that he wouldn't obey. That he did whatever he wanted on his own initiative, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else now. The military police you mentioned, that was headed by Mirzet, did they have uniforms, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That's why I said it was all makeshift. It was all improvised. They may have had a piece or two of a uniform, and maybe Mirzet Halilovic did have a uniform. I don't know where he got it from because I wasn't interested in that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the military police had any special insignia?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have uniforms, let alone insignia of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you saw and experienced while working in the War Presidency and your contacts with Bogilovic, Nurija Jusufovic, Mirzet Halilovic, who in your opinion had influence or control over the police, both the civilian and military police?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Do you mean who was --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, who was superior to them? Who was their chief?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Becir Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Becir Bogilovic have a superior?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. His superior was Hajrudin Avdic, the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you saw, do you know what the role of the armed groups of fighters was that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, dear, armed. Their role was only to hold the lines around the free territory of Srebrenica municipality. That was the role of the defenders who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to my question when I said armed, you responded. What were you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain this word, "Armed." If you have one rifle to ten fighters, that's not -- it was all so meagre, so impoverished. The people lacked clothing, footwear, but they had to be there at the lines to protect their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I will ask you something about Mirzet Halilovic. You knew him personally, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met Mirzet Halilovic when he came to see Mr. Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How would you describe his personality?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He was a young man and he was very nice. He looked very, very nice, and I heard from others that he was a very nice man. He was even a sportsman before the war. During the war, whether it was because of the influence of the war or something else, he started drinking a lot of alcohol and when he got drunk, everybody said his personality changed completely. He was like someone else. He couldn't control himself let alone anybody else. When he was not drunk, when he wasn't drinking alcohol, then he was a very nice man.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed him a commander?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: It was the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear whether Mr. Avdic knew about Halilovic's drinking and did he drink before his appointment?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't. Had he known he would certainly not have appointed because Mr. Avdic was a clever man. He was a wise person and he would never have appointed a man had he known that he would get drunk and act like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did he try to influence him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He often summoned him to his office and spoke to him and he would make promises and excuses, but he never kept his word.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall an incident in the summer of 1992 that had to do with Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember. I remember Mr. Hajrudin summoned Mr. Halilovic because he had heard, received a report, that some men had fired shots at Potocari. As we were very short of ammunition, ammunition was used very carefully, and to waste a few bullets was a disaster. So he sent Mirzet to confiscate the weapons from those young men. However, when Mirzet arrived in Potocari, these men chased him away and they didn't give him anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he beat anyone up or don't you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I think he did beat one of the young men up because they had a quarrel when he arrived to confiscate their weapons. I think he beat a young man up, and I remember that there was a quarrel that broke out and even in the municipal War Presidency, there was discussion of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like a new video clip to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's rather long so we can do it after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. We will have a 30-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I resume my examination-in-chief, I would kindly ask that the translation of D986 be replaced with a new translation, because there is an error. Instead of Hajrudin Avdic, the translation says "Hajrudin Dudic," whereas the original says Hajrudin Avdic. And the word "appointment" is -- next to the word it's written "unclear," although the word transpires quite clearly from the document. It's D986. We merely want to submit the correct translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is the case, if that is the case, we have already -- this came up earlier at some point in time, and we -- in our document, the one we have in our personal record, we've already made that correction. So at least that, from that point of view, you can put your mind at rest. Yes. During the testimony of Smajlovic on 8th of December. All right, but, however, I do agree with you that I think in order to be correct, it should be replaced with a proper translation. Since this is a Defence Exhibit, I think you need to provide us with the alternative translation yourself. Okay? Thank you. And we will replace it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Ms. Vidovic, before you put the question, I've just been informed by the representative of the Registry, the Court officer, that the Prosecution has indeed returned P561 to the Registry. In other words, it's back to us. All right? Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Wubben. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, we talked about the incident in Potocari. I asked that a new video clip be played.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we do that at this time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please follow the video carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall this session of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This session of the War Presidency, does it concern the incident in Potocari you talked about or not?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The incident was discussed at this very session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who filmed the session?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mustafa Sacirovic, also known as Mule, did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, at the very start of the footage, do you recall that the speaker says, "We made the decision whereby the military police should prevent any unnecessary shooting because of shortage of ammunition." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the War Presidency ever taking such a decision?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The War Presidency took several such decisions but they were not fully observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could also hear the same speaker say that from 10 to 5.00 curfew is on. Nobody should move around, and so on.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was a curfew ever introduced in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were no conditions in place for that. On several occasions, there were attempts at introducing a curfew to reduce movement at night. However, due to the very high influx of refugees in Srebrenica, it was impossible to implement this. People were constantly on the move, especially at night, in search of food. You have to understand that people lived in the streets, outdoors. They made makeshift shelters in the town parks. How can you ban them from moving around?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At what point in time was there discussion about the introduction of a curfew at the sessions of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of July, when I started working for the War Presidency, they discussed the introduction of a curfew. However, it proved impossible to implement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that you closely and repeatedly reviewed this video clip during proofing?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the man who says, "Here are representatives from Potocari. Let them have -- take the floor. They don't find Mirza palatable because he beat up one of their own lot"? Do you recall who that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's Hamdija Fejzic, president of the executive committee of the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please play the tape back to the beginning and to stop at 003? I would like the witness to identify some of the persons appearing on the footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the man at the bottom right side of the still, wearing a yellow shirt, who seems to be writing something?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do. That's Resid Efendic, who was secretary of the municipal War Presidency at the time, and he kept minutes at meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, because we need to put this for the record, is there a way in which I can identify this clip for the record? It is at 0003. Yes. Well, there are two indications. The video is paused at 0003, and on the screen were a number of individuals, all males are shown including the gentleman with his back to us wearing a yellow shirt. There are the words, "First speaker: And the shooting started full stop. There if there is a cause for celebration, comma, it is logical, comma, we decided," and it stops there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The person just described by His Honour, was recognised by you as Resid Efendic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who are the people seated next to him, to the right?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Jusuf Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And next to Jusuf Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Avdo Hasanovic, manager of the general war hospital in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can we play the tape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One -- no, no, wait before you play the tape because we need to identify these one after the other. Jusuf Halilovic, is he the one with the light blue shirt? Is he the one nearest to Resid Efendic, in other words? Immediately next to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And is the other one, Avdo Hasanovic, the one next to Jusuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can see his arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. All right. That's fine. Yes, Ms. Vidovic, you may proceed with the rest of the tape and questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the clip be played up until 0010?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, who is the bearded man in the left hand corner of the still?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: That's the president of the municipal War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the record, we are at 00.10, and the person identified by the witness is wearing a horizontal-striped shirt and has a beard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play the video further up until 0056?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you identify these men?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the tape be played back a moment back, to see the person on the left-hand side? We can't see his face. That's the person -- the first person to the left. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who is the person wearing a white shirt, with what is apparently a mustache?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: That is Zulfo Tursunovic, also known as Cica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record we are still at 00.54 and the person identified by the witness is the second one from the left. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who is seated next to Zulfo Tursunovic, to his right, or rather that's his left, to his left side?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: That's Senahid Tabakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are still at 00.54, and the person identified by the witness is the person wearing what seems to be either blue or green dress, sitting to the left of the person previously identified as Zulfo Tursunovic. On the screen, this new person identified as Tabakovic would be the third one from the left and the second one from the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the person seated on the far right?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean this person in this bright-coloured T-shirt? That was the person in the company of Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not referring to the person next to Zulfo Tursunovic but I'm talking about the person seated next to Senahid Tabakovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I misunderstood you. Are you referring to the person with a beard in the yellow T-shirt? That's Akif Krdzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we see the person seat the next to Krdzic, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. For the record while we are still at 00.54, the person identified as Krdzic by the person is the first person from the right wearing a beard and also a yellow T-shirt or short-sleeved shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who is the person seated next to the person you identify as Akif Krdzic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: That's Hamdija Fejzic president of the executive committee of the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, just give me a chance. We are now at still 00.56 and the person identified as Hamdija Fejzic by the witness is the first one from the right wearing a dark, what seems to be a black or very dark-blue polo shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play the tape several seconds ahead to 0103?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you identify the man seated next to Hamdija Fejzic in a blue shirt?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's Aziz Nekic, also a member of the municipal War Presidency, who worked on humanitarian aid, as soon as it started arriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, we are at 01.03 and the person identified as Mr. Nekic is the person with the blue shirt sitting in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you identify the person in the corner of the still with the mustache and a yellow shirt?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's Hamed Alic. I was unable to recall his name earlier. He was the chief of information. He worked on communication so he worked with ham radio operators in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are still at 01.03 and the person identified is the person with a mustache and a yellow shirt, extreme right of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in connection with this meeting I'll ask you the following: Do you recall whether at this session of the War Presidency, Naser was present?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. As I said previously, Naser did not attend every meeting. In fact, he attended meetings only rarely because the situation did not permit him to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why, did you have any knowledge about the situation in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every day we heard shelling in Potocari - Potocari is not far from Srebrenica - because there were constant attacks from Bratunac and this was the front line. Bratunac-Potocari. He had to be there. The people demanded protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Here we have heard and seen that the War Presidency was discussing Mirzet Halilovic and the military police. Previously you told us that you knew that Mirzet Halilovic was appointed by the War Presidency. Please, this incident being discussed here, was it the only incident discussed involving Mirzet Halilovic or not, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not the only such incident. As I've already said, Mr. Halilovic, Mirzet Halilovic, would sometimes drink alcohol and then he would cause incidents, he would get into fights with anyone. If anyone spoke to him he would beat them up. He mainly beat up Muslims because they were there, close at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, was Mirzet Halilovic replaced?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was discussion of that more than once, and finally he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal War Presidency, which had appointed him. The same people who appointed him also relieved him of his duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know the reason for his replacement?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't, but I assume it was because of the incidents and the complaints.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't interested. It wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Is Mirzet Halilovic still alive or is he dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on, I wish to tender this video into evidence. May it be given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is this a video that was handed to you by the Prosecution or did you procure it yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a video made by Mr. Sacirovic, our witness, Mustafa Sacirovic, and we procured it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So this -- and there is -- what we have seen is the entire video or is -- are there any other parts that we haven't seen?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the entire -- or, rather, we have a tape with various clips on it, but if you mean have we edited it in any way, no, we haven't. We have played the entire section. We haven't changed anything in the part we are using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask my learned friends and the Trial Chamber two things. The Prosecution would like to have a copy of this video, what's been shown today. And just to clarify, we are under the impression that the Defence is entering a transcript, not only the visual portion but also what we saw as transcript underneath. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't think either of the two issues you raised create a problem. I take it you will attend to those, Ms. Vidovic. In other words to provide the Prosecution with a copy of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The clip we used, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have already prepared it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you very much. And this will become Defence Exhibit D1003. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now move on and ask you something about the military police and the police in general. Do you recall, after the replacement of Mirzet Halilovic, to the best of your knowledge, did someone else take up his post? Was someone else appointed?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Atif Krdzic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who appointed Atif Krdzic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We saw Atif Krdzic on this video clip of the War Presidency. Tell Their Honours what his profession was, even before he was appointed instead of Mirzet Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He had been a policeman before the war, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, to whom was Krdzic subordinate?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: To Becir Bogilovic, the chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the basis for your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Because the military police existed only on paper and they were part of the civilian police, and whenever something was needed by the police, it was always Becir who came or Nurija Jusufovic and even Krdzic would come.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Krdzic come to the War Presidency to attend meetings together with Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, until when did the military police remain part of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Until the demilitarisation of Srebrenica in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who then became chief of police?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Hakija Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you had occasion to work with him, with Hakija Meholjic, right after demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: About a week later. He asked Hamdija if I could type something for him. He needed assistance. So I spent one day in his office typing all day, as a temporary assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he was writing something that had to do with police, the military police, Krdzic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: He was asking for the military police to be disbanded. In fact, it hardly existed. There were just a few men in it, including Atif Krdzic, and he wanted Atif Krdzic to stop working. I don't know why. But he didn't want him to continue working, and he said he didn't want to work with him and couldn't work in his service any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll move on now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness two documents, P11 and P12.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please first look at this document, P11, dated the 27th of November 1992. In the heading, it says, "Srebrenica armed forces staff." The signature is allegedly that of Osman Osmanovic. And it says at its session of the 22nd of November 1992 the Srebrenica OS staff issued the following decision on reorganising the military police. Do you know anything about this reorganisation? Did you hear of it?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the arrival of Atif Krdzic, did you observe any difference in the police, any difference in the contacts between the police and Hajrudin Avdic? In other words, did Krdzic continue to work in the same way as Halilovic had done?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I think the situation was the same, yes. Nothing changed with the arrival of Atif Krdzic and with the replacement of Mirzet Halilovic. I think the situation remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please have another look at the date. It says the 27th of November 1992. Did you know Osman Osmanovic well?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Osman Osmanovic was a great friend of my husband's. He was a family friend. He came to our home.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, on the 27th of November 1992, was he in Srebrenica at all?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he wasn't. He came to see us on the 24th of November on our wedding anniversary. He visited my husband and me. He didn't know it was our anniversary but he had come to say goodbye because he was leaving for Gorazde. He was being sent by Hajrudin Avdic as some sort of commissioner and he was going to Gorazde and he had to leave on the following day, the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did he go?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He did go on the 25th of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So do you believe he could have signed this decision on the 27th of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: I think he couldn't have because he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at the other document, P12. I will read it to you. It says here, "Military police commander, Atif Krdzic, is hereby authorised" and so on. I will not put any questions to you about the content of the decision because you ever told us you were not aware of any reorganisation. But look at the date, please, the 6th of December 1992. To the best of your knowledge, was Osman Osmanovic in Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. He couldn't have been because he left on the 25th of November to go to Gorazde and he returned only in March 1993. Because when he came back, he came to say hello. He said he hadn't been able to get back because of the heavy snow and the severe winter. The Serbs had strengthened their lines and a lot of men who tried to cross between the lines came to harm.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now look at the form of both these decisions, P11 and P12. Previously, you said that the decisions you typed out, and you showed us an example, were written in a certain form. Is it evident from these decisions whether they were delivered to anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No. In my view, no. I would not consider such a decision as complete, as having been completed or sent to anyone because it doesn't say to whom it was sent, who received it, who delivered it, on either of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For this decision to be implemented, to the best of your knowledge of how things functioned, when decisions in general were issued, was this registered somewhere that they were delivered?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It would be registered that they were delivered to so and so. If they were natural persons, their names would be entered. If they were legal entities then the name of the organ or organisation would be entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does either of these decisions show that they were put in the archives, for example?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA DJILOVIC
utterances.text: No, because it doesn't say anywhere that they were delivered to the archives or to anyone. It's not there on these decisions. So in my view, these decisions are only drafts or they are incomplete. They are not finished, they are not complete decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can put them away. Could the witness be shown document P5 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies, P608.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this might be a convenient moment to stop. Unfortunately we have lost a little time today but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I'll need more than half an hour to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Sellers, what about your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will take all of tomorrow and there is always that it might just go over a bit to the next day also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Do you think it is necessary that we start earlier than 9.00 tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we leave ourselves in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honours. We agree to start earlier in order to finish with the witness tomorrow, for the witness's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 8.30 tomorrow morning instead of nine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the understanding is that you make, Ms. Sellers, an effort to finish with the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand your understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam, we are finishing here for today because our time has expired. We'll continue tomorrow morning starting a little bit earlier than scheduled, 8.30. The idea is to finish with your testimony tomorrow so that you can go back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime please, between today and tomorrow, you're not to communicate with anyone on the matters that you are testifying upon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of January, 2006, at 8.30 a.m. 23 24 25
